title: TeamWork: Role-Aware Anomaly Detection in Time Series
one_liner: The paper treats variables in multivariate time series differently—ranking them by how much they disrupt the system when they go wrong—and masks different time scales to learn both short and long patterns.
lead: In a multivariate time series, not all variables matter equally. Some are drivers that move the whole system; others provide supporting context. This paper ranks variables by their importance to the system and treats them differently when learning anomalies. It also learns temporal patterns at multiple scales by masking (hiding) parts of the data in different period windows.

paras: A multivariate time series is just a table where each row is a moment in time and each column tracks something different—temperature, pressure, voltage, valve position. Anomalies (breaks, faults, unusual behavior) can happen in any column.

The naive approach treats all columns the same: learn what normal looks like, then flag anything that deviates. But this fails because columns are not equal. Some columns drive the whole system (if they jump, everything jumps). Others are passengers (they react, but do not initiate). Anomalies in driver columns break the system catastrophically. Anomalies in passenger columns are noise. A method that learns from all columns equally will miss the architecture of the system itself.

Also, anomalies live at different time scales. A brief glitch (one reading off) is different from a slow drift (creeping wrongness over hours). Existing methods learn one temporal pattern and miss multi-scale anomalies.

callout.html: Rank variables by how much they matter to the system, treat them differently, and learn anomalies at multiple time scales.

panels.title: 1. Normal multivariate system
panels.caption: Five variables all moving in sync: driver (first three) plus supporting variables.

panels.title: 2. One driver breaks
panels.caption: When the first column jumps wrong, three others collapse. Anomaly cascades.

panels.title: 3. Rank by importance
panels.caption: The paper scores each variable by how much it disrupts others when it breaks.

panels.title: 4. Role-aware interaction
panels.caption: Drivers update strongly; auxiliaries add detail. Model learns the true hierarchy.

panels.title: 5. Multi-scale masking
panels.caption: Hide different time windows to force learning short glitches and long drifts separately.

steps.text: Measure how much each variable drives the others; call this its uncertainty-reduction contribution.
Split variables into dominant (high score) and auxiliary (low score).
Dominant variables flow strongly into the model; auxiliary variables are gated (multiplied down) to be contextual.
Hide stretches of time (short periods, medium, long) to force learning anomalies at each scale.
Measure if the real data deviates from the learned normal pattern; flag the biggest breaks.

paras: The paper changes how variables are weighted in the neural network. Instead of treating all variables equally, it assigns each variable a role (dominant or auxiliary) and gates their signals accordingly.

hidden.name: uncertainty reduction per variable
paras: Each variable contributes differently to predicting the future. The paper measures how much each variable reduces the overall surprise (entropy) about what comes next. A variable that always pins down the future is dominant; one that barely constrains it is auxiliary.
The paper estimates this by looking at how much each variable's information helps predict other variables. High score means the variable drives others; low score means it is mostly reacting.

heat.caption: Darker means higher uncertainty reduction (drives the system). Bordered cells are ranked dominant.

reads.html: The paper asks: if we remove this variable, how much harder does the system become to predict? A driver variable matters; an auxiliary one is nice to have but not essential.
The paper computes uncertainty reduction via information-theoretic scoring (e.g., using mutual information or reconstruction loss contribution) and thresholds to assign roles.

mechanism.h2: Why treating roles differently catches anomalies
paras: A multivariate system is hierarchical: drivers constrain the space of possibilities, auxiliaries fill in details. When learning normal patterns, if all variables are weighted equally, the model divides its learning effort equally across noise and signal. It learns a blurry average instead of the true structure.

By upweighting drivers and gating auxiliaries, the model builds a skeleton of the system (which variables are core, which react). This skeleton is sparse and unmoved by noise: small errors in an auxiliary variable do not flip predictions of the driver pattern, because drivers carry almost all the weight. When a driver goes wrong, the model has learned that it is shocking, because it broke a heavily-weighted pattern. When an auxiliary goes wrong, it is expected noise.

Masking at multiple periods forces the model to separately learn glitches (one or two bad readings) from drifts (slow creep over hours). A glitch is flagged because it violates the short-period pattern; a drift is flagged because it violates the long-period pattern. Without multi-period masking, the model averages these two and misses both.

stages.s: Raw multivariate time series (all variables raw)
Compute uncertainty reduction score per variable
Gate: scale auxiliary signals down via multiplication
Learn normal at multiple period masks (1hr, 1day, 1week)

math.words: loss = recon_loss_short + recon_loss_medium + recon_loss_long + importance_weight * (dominant_scale * driver_penalty + auxiliary_scale * auxiliary_penalty)
math.equation: L = (1/N) * sum_t ||x_t - x_hat_t||^2 + lambda * sum_i importance_i * (w_i^d * d_i + w_i^a * a_i)
symbols: predicted normal reading at time t
uncertainty reduction score for variable i (high=driver, low=auxiliary)
weight for driver role (e.g., 1.0 for dominant variables)
weight for auxiliary role (e.g., 0.2 for auxiliary variables)
deviation of variable i from driver pattern
deviation of variable i from auxiliary pattern
how much to penalize role-violating changes

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Dominant weight w^d = 1.0, auxiliary weight w^a = 0.3.
At time t, variable 1 (dominant, importance 8) deviates 0.5 from pattern: penalty = 8 * 1.0 * 0.5 = 4.0.
At time t, variable 4 (auxiliary, importance 1) deviates 0.5 from pattern: penalty = 1 * 0.3 * 0.5 = 0.15.
Same deviation size, but driver is penalized 26× harder, so training leaves driver on pattern.
Over three period masks (short, medium, long), total loss sums penalties at each scale.
Higher loss at any scale means that time window breaks a learned pattern; flagged as anomaly.

math.note: The equation weights each variable by its learned importance and role, forcing the model to fit drivers tightly and auxiliaries loosely.

charts.title: Naive method (all equal)
charts.note: Equal weighting drowns driver anomalies in auxiliary noise. False positives spike.

charts.title: TeamWork (role-aware)
charts.note: By upweighting drivers, the model learns the true system structure and catches real breaks cleanly.

items.html: If two variables are truly equal partners (neither drives the other), the importance score is ambiguous. The method may misclassify one as auxiliary when it is equally important. Fix: use domain knowledge to seed roles, not just data-driven ranking.

If the system has a long period (e.g., monthly cycle) but the training data is only one month, the long-period mask sees all normal and learns nothing. Anomalies in the rare cycle are missed. Fix: ensure training data spans at least 3 cycles of the longest period.

If the method marks an auxiliary variable as too unimportant, it might ignore correlated anomalies in other auxiliaries that together indicate a real problem. Fix: lower the auxiliary gate weight (e.g., 0.5 instead of 0.2) to keep some sensitivity.
Combine data-driven importance ranking with domain knowledge of the system. Tune period masks to the system's natural rhythms. Validate role assignments on labeled anomaly data before deployment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic multivariate time series: a simple linear model where 3 variables drive 2 others. Inject anomalies: a large jump in a driver (should be caught because the model learned drivers are heavily weighted and carry the system pattern) and a slow drift in an auxiliary (harder to catch without multi-period masking, because it blends into normal auxiliary noise—but the long-period mask forces the model to learn slow trends separately, so it is caught). Compare: (1) baseline model treating all variables equally, (2) the role-aware model. Measure detection rate for driver vs. auxiliary anomalies and false alarm rate.
demo.metric_eq: detection_rate_driver = (anomalies_in_drivers_caught) / (total_driver_anomalies); false_alarm_rate = (normal_windows_flagged) / (total_normal_windows); role_aware should beat baseline on both.
demo.closing: The demo must show that upweighting drivers and multi-scale masking together catch real driver anomalies that the naive method misses, without a flood of false alarms in the auxiliary variables.
